input.description: Reedholm boy of about fourteen, an eel-trapper's son, who carried the first marsh-fever cases to Stonebridge market a week ago and went home sick. Brannoc plans to ask for him first at Reedholm.

entries.text: notebook: created an entry for Sedge; added 1 relationship to Sedge

Ansel takes your hand in both of his. "The book stays open," he says. "Write if you can. If you can't, come back and tell it yourself." You trace a blessing on the green door, and it feels like leaving a house you've lived in a good deal longer than six days.

On Sedge: yes, he's a sound first name to ask for. He carried the sickness out of Reedholm and knows who fell ill first and where he walked, which tells you more than any rumour. But a fourteen-year-old who went home sick may be the worst off by now, or past asking. Ask for him, and look at the village as you go.

The river road south is long and level, with the water slow and brown beside it, and the fields give way to rough pasture, then to alder carr. You eat the heel of bread on the move. By four in the afternoon you reach the Eel Fork, a wooden milestone grey with weather, with the east branch dropping away onto a raised causeway of packed earth and split logs. The air changes here, cooler and wetter, smelling of mud and rotting reed. Beyond the first bend, the land falls flat and silver to the horizon, all reeds and still water, with a heron standing in the shallows like a post.

It's eleven minutes past four on Day 11. You've walked about eight and a half hours, and the causeway is ahead, with perhaps two hours of light left. Reedholm is a day further, past the Black Ford. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and willow-bark for the first fevers.

What does Brannoc do?

sheet.name: Brannoc Ashdown
sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

features: Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 3: 15 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

Ansel takes your hand at the green door and says the book will stay open for Reedholm's names, and that he'll pray for the road. You bless the lintel with two fingers, the old way, and go.

The river road south is new to you. The valley flattens and the air turns damp. Alders crowd the bank, and the fields give way to rough pasture, then to reed and standing water. A heron lifts from a ditch and flaps off like a folded umbrella. You keep a steady pace and eat Ansel's bread as you walk. By a little before four you reach the Eel Fork, a grey wooden milestone leaning in the grass with two arms cut in it. The east arm is marked with a crude eel, and a raised causeway of packed earth and stones runs off across the water between the reeds.

Your answer: yes. Sedge is a good first name to ask for. He is the one who carried the fever to market, and he went home sick. His mother is an eel-trapper named Marra Teel, so you can ask for her too. The carters knew no more than that, and I won't claim they did.

It's twenty to four on Day 11. You have about two hours of light, four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, two lanterns, and a night's walk or camp ahead of you. The causeway to the Black Ford is a long, narrow road with water on both sides, and the Wick-fires are said to show on moonless nights.

input.description: Boy of Reedholm, about fourteen, who carried eels to the Stonebridge market and brought the first marsh-fever cases there; went home sick. Possibly the best first contact in Reedholm, if he is still alive.

entries.text: notebook: created an entry for Sedge; added 1 relationship to Sedge

Ansel presses the bread and the twist of willow-bark into your hands, and you bless his green door with your palm on the lintel. "The book will be open," he says. "Write if you can. And come back, Edda's boy."

The river road south is wide and well rutted at first, then thins to a single track between pollard willows. By midday the hills are low behind you and the land is flat and wet, with the river wide and slow on your left. You pass a few farms with their doors shut and a shepherd who watches you out of sight. You walk steadily, eat your bread on the move, and keep your eye on the reeds, which sway with no wind in them more than once. Nothing comes out.

By half past four you reach a wooden milestone, silvered by weather, with a carved eel on its face. This is the Eel Fork. The west branch runs on along the river. The east one turns onto a raised causeway of packed earth and brushwood, with black water on both sides and a mist already gathering. Reedholm is two days along it, by the carters' count. The light is good for another hour, and the first night's camping place is a dry mound a mile along the causeway, with a few stunted alders.

As to your question: yes. Sedge is as good a first name to ask for as any. He carried the fever to market, he knows who fell sick first, and he will know the village's paths. You can't know whether he's alive. A boy who took ill a week ago may be mending or worse, and I'll not pretend you know more than the carters told you.

It's twenty to five on Day 11. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, two lanterns, rope, and thirty-seven flasks of oil. You are 1,100 XP in, and the causeway goes on into the evening.

sheet.name: Brannoc Ashdown
sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

traits: I am warm and patient with the sick and frightened, and I hum hymns while I work.

features: Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 3: 15 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

spellcasting.notes: Prepare up to 6 spells from the whole cleric list after a long rest (domain spells are always prepared and don't count).
